Revised assessment: The FOMC’s decision to hold the federal funds rate at 5.25–5.50% and continue balance-sheet runoff signals a slightly hawkish but balanced stance—acknowledging solid growth and labor strength while emphasizing that inflation remains elevated and that tighter credit will weigh on activity. This is consistent with Taylor-rule guidance and the Taylor principle (Taylor; Woodford) that call for a restrictive policy rate when inflation exceeds target. The explicit focus on tighter credit conditions reflects the credit channel literature (Bernanke and coauthors; Kashyap) in which bank lending frictions amplify monetary restraint and dampen output and inflation. Ongoing QT can lift term premiums and affect long-term yields (Cochrane; Piazzesi), reinforcing restrictive financial conditions. The attention to inflation expectations and communication aligns with inflation-targeting and sticky-information frameworks (Mankiw and Reis), while the emphasis on lags and uncertainty echoes real-time policy challenges highlighted by Orphanides. The statement’s reassurance that the banking system is “sound and resilient” is modestly positive, but the inflation vigilance tilts the tone toward cautious restraint.
